name: MTGEMM-A
baseline: Apple Accelerate sgemm/dgemm (also OpenBLAS develop and 0.3.34, Eigen master, LIBXSMM, KleidiAI)
workload: FP32/FP64 GEMM on Apple M4 Pro using Arm SME2: the paper's 24 workloads and square sizes 512-4096, row- and column-major, one thread and default threading, geometric mean GFLOPS.
claimed_speedup: FP32 geomean 2777 vs 2363 GFLOPS for Accelerate on the paper's 24 column-major workloads at default threading (1.18x); 1.19x (column-major) and 1.26x (row-major) on one thread for the paper's 24 workloads; 1.25x row-major / 1.19x column-major vs Accelerate in the paper-comparison table; 3.7x faster than OpenBLAS 0.3.34 (row-major) and 2.2x faster than LIBXSMM (column-major), 1.7x faster than KleidiAI (one thread); Eigen master 1044 GFLOPS vs 2777 at default threading
hardware: Apple M4 Pro, 8 performance cores in two clusters of 4 (two SME units, SVL 512 bits), 48 GB
tradeoffs: Apple M4-family (SME2) only for the SME backend; an AMX backend covers M2/M3-class chips; no transposed operands (computes C = alpha A B + beta C only); GEMM only, not full BLAS; macOS cannot pin threads to an SME cluster so two-thread results depend on scheduling.
caveats: Reproduction of the paper arXiv:2512.21473 (MpGEMM, whose authors released no code), by a single author, measured on one machine (8 P-core M4 Pro vs the paper's 10 P-core); at default threading it is slower than Accelerate on 10 of 484 shapes; the OpenBLAS 0.3.34 figure in the LIBXSMM/KleidiAI comparison is one Homebrew-build measurement that falls back to NEON at M=4096; OpenBLAS develop's own SME kernels reach 0.50x-0.78x of MTGEMM-A on one thread. The repo also carries an OpenBLAS port (branch sme2-gemm of the author's OpenBLAS fork, not yet submitted) and an Eigen SME GEMM backend developed from this code. Wave 8 leads.md already lists this repo as a candidate for the MpGEMM paper entry.
found_via: Wave 8 leads.md (from the MpGEMM verifier); GitHub repository search 'SME GEMM Apple Silicon'; opened the repo page and README.

name: cpu_gemm_opt
baseline: OpenBLAS 0.3.4 sgemm (README: 'most of the size exceed openblas(0.3.4)'; the driver times cblas_sgemm from the OpenBLAS it links)
workload: Single-core row-major SGEMM, square sizes 48 to 3264, alpha=beta=1, hand-written AVX2 6x16 micro-kernel with per-size tuned block parameters, hyperthreading off.
claimed_speedup: 78.31 GFLOPS (96.38% of peak) vs 75.11 for the reference column at 960^3; 78.12 vs 73.65 at 1920^3; 78.20 vs 73.41 at 3264^3; 75.79 vs 68.14 at 192^3; 60.13 vs 43.05 at 48^3. About 4-7% faster at sizes from 960 up (derived from page data). Slower than the reference at 144^3 (55.85 vs 64.26).
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6142, one core at 2600 MHz, hyperthreading off, theoretical 81.25 GFLOPS (AVX2 FMA)
tradeoffs: SGEMM only, single core, row-major driver; AVX2 kernel (the Xeon Gold 6142 also has AVX-512, which it does not use); needs a per-machine tuned parameter database (sgemm_tuned.db), hyperthreading off and ideally turbo off to reach peak.
caveats: OpenBLAS is version 0.3.4 (2019) and its build TARGET is not stated, so it may not have been the best kernel for that CPU; the gflops_ref column is not labelled in the README (identified as OpenBLAS from the README sentence and the driver/build script); the win is small (a few percent) and reverses at some sizes below 768; the README says it is still being tuned; results are 7 years old.
found_via: GitHub repository search 'beats OpenBLAS'; opened the repo page, README and src/build.sh.

name: emugemm-cdna
baseline: rocBLAS native FP32 sgemm on AMD MI250 (per-shape tuned solutions)
workload: FP32 GEMM emulated by splitting inputs into three BF16 slices (bf16x3) multiplied on the matrix cores, on one MI250 GCD, across the tested shapes, with the native rocBLAS side also tuned per shape.
claimed_speedup: 1.20-1.22x faster than native FP32 on every shape tested, after per-shape solution tuning of both sides (README table).
tradeoffs: Not bit-compatible with FP32: accuracy floor of 4.4355e-6 relative error with the bf16x3 scheme, with a request API (max_rel_err) that reports 'TARGET UNREACHABLE' instead of silently under-delivering; only gfx90a was tested; needs a tuning table per GPU and ROCm version; speed ceiling on MI250 is 1.33x.
caveats: GPU, not CPU. The README itself records that an earlier 2.1x was really 1.21x because the baseline ran rocBLAS's default kernel, and ties the investigation to ROCm/rocm-libraries issue 9985 (rocBLAS default solution losing to another solution in the same library), so the win depends on how well the native baseline is tuned. Written with AI assistance (commits co-authored by an AI assistant). Baseline rocBLAS is not one of OpenBLAS, MKL, Eigen or BLIS.
found_via: GitHub repository search 'topic:gemm language:C++'; opened the repo page, README and build example.

name: COSMA
baseline: Intel MKL ScaLAPACK pdgemm (also Cray LibSci, Cray LibSci_acc, CARMA, CTF)
workload: Distributed matrix-matrix multiplication (communication-optimal, with a ScaLAPACK pxgemm wrapper): CP2K RPA benchmark of 128 water molecules (46 tall-and-skinny pdgemm calls) and square matrices, on Piz Daint.
claimed_speedup: README: 'speedups by factor of up to 8.3x over the second-fastest algorithm'; 'approximately 2x faster' than Cray-libsci_acc for CP2K pdgemm on 1024 GPU nodes; GPU version '25-27% faster than the second best' on 128 nodes (MKL, Cray-libsci, libsci_acc compared); CPU COSMA reaches peak and is compared against Intel MKL ScaLAPACK 19.0.1.144 on square matrices (plots).
hardware: Piz Daint (Cray XC50 GPU nodes and XC40 CPU nodes), 128 and 1024 nodes
tradeoffs: MPI-based, needs a local BLAS (MKL, LibSci, OpenBLAS, BLIS, cuBLAS, rocBLAS) and optionally ScaLAPACK for the wrapper; distributed-memory only; speedups depend on matrix shape and node count; the ScaLAPACK-layout wrapper costs some throughput versus the native layout.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (SC19 Best Student Paper, ACM DL link in README) but this run could not open the paper, so the numbers cited are the README's; the 8.3x is over the second-fastest algorithm (not necessarily MKL); the result tables are SVG images; compiler and flags are not stated on the README; results are from 2019 with MKL 19.0.1.144 and Cray LibSci 19.06/19.10.
found_via: WebFetch of github.com/eth-cscs/spla README which links COSMA; GitHub topics/matrix-multiplication?l=c++ page; then the COSMA README.

name: cbk (Compact Batch Kernels)
baseline: Intel MKL compact kernels (mkl_dgeqrf_compact, mkl_dpotrf_compact, mkl_dtrsm_compact pipeline) and per-matrix LAPACKE (LAPACKE_dgels, LAPACKE_dposv, LAPACKE_dgeqrf)
workload: Batched QR, Cholesky and unpivoted LDL^T factorizations and solves for pools of many small double-precision matrices (n=10..120) in the compact interleaved layout, one thread.
claimed_speedup: QR solve (1000 matrices, n=10..120, 1 RHS): cbk gels 2.7x geometric mean over LAPACKE_dgels (1.5x at n=100) and cbk-batch 1.25x over MKL-batch; at 64 RHS the gels win drops to 1.3x and cbk-batch to 1.12x over MKL. SPD solve (512 matrices, 1 RHS): fused compact solve 2-9x over LAPACKE_dposv at orders 8-48, 1.4-2.2x at 60-105, geometric mean 1.7x, level with MKL's compact pipeline (0.9-1.0x geomean).
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 -march=native (CMake Release); MKL compact paths linked against sequential MKL, all paths driven with the same thread count
tradeoffs: Needs the compact (interleaved) layout and packing; many small matrices only; the win disappears for larger matrices; unpivoted LDL^T (no Bunch-Kaufman pivoting); optional MKL-compatible API layer; GCC/Clang vector extensions, OpenMP over groups of V matrices.
caveats: Hardware is not identified beyond '4-core AVX-512 container', so tier C; the benchmark page labels the runs 'indicative'; pack/unpack time is excluded from the timed region; per-matrix LAPACK wins from about n=128-168 (0.25x at n=256) and at nrhs=64 is level or ahead at several sizes; SPD solve only matches MKL compact; the README states most of the library, tests and benchmarks were written by Claude models with human review. The LAPACKE backend used in the baseline is not named on the page.
found_via: GitHub repository search 'topic:lapack language:C++'; opened the repo page, README, CHANGELOG and examples/BENCHMARKS.md.

name: MaxMulSK
baseline: OpenBLAS (develop build reaching its own SME kernels, one thread) and Apple Accelerate (pinned to one thread)
workload: Single-threaded FP32 row-major GEMM on Apple M4 with Arm SME/SME2: 35 shapes (squares, LLM-shaped, DeepSeek-V3 and LLaMA), allocation, packing and writeback included in every timed call, geometric mean of paired ratios.
claimed_speedup: v5.1 (development kernel, code not published): 1.86x tuned OpenBLAS (ahead on 33 of 35 shapes, tied on 256^3 and 512^3), 1.16x Apple Accelerate (ahead by >5% on 29 shapes, 0.74x at 256^3), 1.06x MpGEMM. Published v3 kernel (9 September session): 1.40-1.77 TFLOP/s end to end, 1.01x-1.31x tuned OpenBLAS on squares, 1.36x-2.23x on LLM shapes, 1.05x/1.02x Accelerate at 1024^3/4096^3 and 5-17% behind it elsewhere.
compiler_and_flags: Homebrew LLVM clang (version not stated), -O3 -mcpu=apple-m4 -fopenmp, SME files -march=armv8.7-a+sme+sme2 (CMakeLists.txt)
hardware: Apple M4, macOS 26.6.2, AC power, single thread
tradeoffs: Single-threaded FP32 only; Apple M4 (SME2) only; row-major C = A*B; needs LLVM clang from Homebrew because Apple's bundled clang lacks the SME intrinsics.
caveats: The headline v5.1 numbers are for code that is 'not in this repository yet' (published kernels are v3 and v4c), so the 1.86x and 1.16x cannot be reproduced from the repo; the published-v3 claims can. Homebrew OpenBLAS cannot reach its own SME kernels, so the OpenBLAS baseline is a develop build with OPENBLAS_DIRECT_LIMIT=1792 that the author built; small calls (256^3) depend on what ran just before them and the mechanism is unresolved; one session, two runs, one machine; the author calls it a student's study.
found_via: GitHub repository search 'SME GEMM Apple Silicon'; opened the repo page, README and CMakeLists.txt.

name: GEMM_AVX2_FMA3 (wjc404)
baseline: Intel MKL 2019 update 4 (also MKL 2018) sgemm and dgemm
workload: Large-matrix SGEMM and DGEMM (M=N=K=20000) with AVX2/FMA3 kernels and a Fortran interface, 8 OpenMP threads.
claimed_speedup: SGEMM 963-976 GFLOPS vs MKL2019 944-951; DGEMM 477-481 GFLOPS vs MKL2019 466-469, at M=N=K=20000 (about 1.02-1.03x, derived from page data).
hardware: Intel Core i9-9900K with AVX-offset 6, OMP_NUM_THREADS=8
tradeoffs: AVX2/FMA3 only, Fortran interface with 32-bit integers, large matrices only (title says 'for large matrices'); no AVX-512 or irregular-size tuning in the README.
caveats: Only one problem size is reported; benchmark executables in bench/ are precompiled binaries linked against MKL 2018/2019 (benchmark source not clearly shown), compiler and flags are not stated; MKL 2019 is old; margin is about 2-3%, within run-to-run noise of many systems; repository is archived (August 2019).
found_via: GitHub repository search 'outperforms MKL'; opened the repo page, README and commits page.

name: transpose-scale (hpit)
baseline: Intel MKL 2025.1.0 mkl_simatcopy (in-place transpose with scale); cblas_simatcopy from OpenBLAS on ARM
workload: In-place square float matrix transpose fused with a scale factor, tiled SIMD kernel (AVX2/SSE/NEON), latency and bandwidth percentiles over power-of-two sizes.
claimed_speedup: README: '3-6x faster than MKL' (bandwidth bar chart image, power-of-two sizes).
compiler_and_flags: CMake: -O3 -march=native -ffast-math, C++20; compiler name not stated
tradeoffs: Square in-place transpose with scaling only (BLAS-extension imatcopy), not GEMM; single-precision; AVX2/NEON; no license file.
caveats: No LICENSE file, so code cannot be copied; the numbers appear only in a chart image; the MKL function compared (mkl_simatcopy) is read from the benchmark source, not the README; compiler not named; MKL runs sequential; one CPU.
found_via: GitHub repository search 'faster than MKL'; opened the repo page, README, CMakeLists.txt and utils/time_kernel.cpp.

name: ReLAPACK
baseline: reference LAPACK, OpenBLAS LAPACK routines and Intel MKL LAPACK routines
workload: Recursive implementations of LAPACK compute kernels (LU, Cholesky, triangular inversion, Sylvester and Lyapunov solvers and others) that call BLAS; README says they outperform LAPACK and improve on OpenBLAS and MKL.
claimed_speedup: README: 'ReLAPACK's routines not only outperform the reference LAPACK but also improve upon the performance of tuned implementations, such as OpenBLAS and MKL.' No numbers on the README page.
tradeoffs: Drop-in LAPACK interface (links in front of LAPACK, replaces only the covered routines); needs a BLAS plus LAPACK unblocked kernels underneath; covers only routines where recursion helps (see coverage.md); C code with Fortran-style interfaces.
caveats: The README quantifies nothing. The numbers are in the cited paper, Peise and Bientinesi, 'Recursive Algorithms for Dense Linear Algebra: The ReLAPACK Collection' (arXiv:1602.06763; a search snippet reports publication as ACM TOMS Algorithm 979, vol 44(2), 2017), which this run could not open (arxiv.org, ACM and Semantic Scholar are blocked in this container), so the tier is set from the README claim alone and a verifier with access to the paper could raise it to B or A. Last commit is a typo fix; the code dates from 2016-2017 and compares against OpenBLAS and MKL versions of that era.
found_via: Candidate from domain knowledge (recursive LAPACK); opened github.com/HPAC/ReLAPACK, its README and commits page; WebSearch for the ReLAPACK paper title (paper itself not reachable).

name: SPLA
baseline: Intel MKL ScaLAPACK pdgemm (also COSMA and Cray LibSci_acc)
workload: Distributed tall-and-skinny matrix multiplication (pgemm_ssb stripe-stripe-block) on Piz Daint, CPU nodes 2x18-core Xeon E5-2695 v4 and GPU nodes with Tesla P100.
claimed_speedup: README: on CPU 'performance is much better compared to Intel MKL and similar to COSMA'; on GPU 'SPLA significantly outperforms COSMA and LIBSCI_ACC'; no numbers in text (plots).
hardware: Piz Daint multi-core: 2 x Intel Xeon E5-2695 v4 @ 2.10GHz (2 x 18 cores); Piz Daint GPU: Xeon E5-2690 v3 + NVIDIA Tesla P100 16GB
tradeoffs: MPI plus optional CUDA/ROCm; specific matrix distributions (stripe/block) rather than a general ScaLAPACK pdgemm; C++ and C interfaces; can take device-memory input.
caveats: Plots only, no numeric speedups in the text; compiler and flags not stated; one tall-and-skinny matrix shape family; the MKL baseline is a ScaLAPACK-style call mapped onto the same operation; data from about 2020 on Piz Daint hardware.
found_via: GitHub topics/gemm?l=c++ page, which lists spla; WebFetch of the repo and its README.

name: gemm (johnnyw3, AVX/AMX kernels)
baseline: OpenBLAS or Intel MKL, whichever was faster on each machine (OpenBLAS built with BUILD_BFLOAT16=1 for AMX)
workload: fp32 (AVX2, AVX-512) and bf16-input/fp32-output (AMX) GEMM, n=4096, single-threaded and 4 threads, average of 10 runs.
claimed_speedup: AMX on Granite Rapids Xeon 6972P: 1279 vs 1229 GFLOPS single-threaded (1.04x) and 4810 vs 4675 with 4 threads (1.03x); but slower on AVX2 Kaby Lake i5-8350U (78 vs 103, 0.76x; 213 vs 282 with 4 threads) and AVX-512 Tiger Lake i5-1135G7 (106 vs 122, 0.87x; 380 vs 465 with 4 threads).
compiler_and_flags: clang++ (version not stated; clang 16+ or gcc 13+ required for AMX), -march=$(TARGET) -O3 -flto (Makefile)
hardware: Intel Xeon 6972P (Granite Rapids), Core i5-1135G7 (Tiger Lake), Core i5-8350U (Kaby Lake)
tradeoffs: x86 only (AVX2, AVX-512, AMX); the AMX path takes bf16 inputs; multithreaded code does not scale well beyond 8 threads; README says the best results are single/lightly threaded; no license file.
caveats: Beats the baseline only on AMX hardware (3-4%); on AVX2 and AVX-512 it is 13-24% slower; the baseline is the better of OpenBLAS and MKL chosen per machine; no LICENSE file in the repository, so the code cannot be copied; one size (n=4096); compiler version not stated.
found_via: GitHub repository search 'AMX GEMM'; opened the repo page, README and Makefile.

name: MuBLIS
workload: Level-3 real BLAS operations (GEMM and others) generated from a BLIS-style framework with NEON and AVX2 micro-kernels, single thread, f32, Apple M4.
claimed_speedup: README: matches single-threaded OpenBLAS on 5 of 6 single-threaded L3 real BLAS operations and 'slightly outperforms OpenBLAS' on the Apple M4, reaching ~80% of peak FLOPs for single-threaded GEMM (chart image); also '~20x' over reasonably optimized generic cache-tiled baselines.
hardware: Apple M4 (also tested on Xeon Gold 6248R, Ryzen 7 7700X, i5-7500 per README)
tradeoffs: Framework in which per-microarchitecture micro-kernels are about 200 lines each; ships NEON and AVX2 kernels; L3 BLAS only; single-threaded numbers in the README.
caveats: The margin over OpenBLAS is described as 'slightly' and appears only in a chart image; compiler, flags and OpenBLAS version are not stated; match rather than beat on 5 of 6 operations; the same author's fast_matmul repo says its single-threaded kernel is 'comparable' to OpenBLAS with a difference too small to measure, and claims a faster multithreaded version without numbers.
found_via: GitHub repository search 'outperforms OpenBLAS' (surfaced NinjadenMu/fast_matmul, whose README links MuBLIS); opened the MuBLIS repo page and README.

name: gpu-compute (SGEMM for Blackwell)
baseline: cuBLAS cublasSgemm with CUBLAS_PEDANTIC_MATH (true FP32) on an RTX 5080
workload: Hand-written row-major FP32 SGEMM, square sizes N=32 to 256 (and larger sizes for contrast), timed with CUDA events and checked against cublasSgemm; a 32x32-tile kernel runs one to 64 CTAs.
claimed_speedup: Faster than cuBLAS FP32 on every square N from 32 to 256 measured: 8.1 us vs 16.5 us at 32^3 (2.02x), 9.5 vs 16.2 us at 64^3 (1.71x), 10.9 vs 16.2 us at 128^3 (1.49x), 11.9 vs 16.9 us at 192^3 (1.42x), 13.6 vs 17.8 us at 256^3 (1.30x). Not a win on tall-skinny shapes (4096x64x4096 is 0.90x), and at 4096^3 the README's throughput table (units not labelled) shows the auto kernel at 23.05 vs 36.79 for cuBLAS FP32.
compiler_and_flags: nvcc from CUDA 13.3 via CMake, C++17, --use_fast_math -lineinfo --expt-relaxed-constexpr, CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=native; Windows PowerShell build script
tradeoffs: Only wins in the launch-bound small-square regime (N<=256, used up to about 384); loses on large and tall-skinny shapes; fixed 32x32 tile with one output per thread; row-major C = A@B; includes a labelled WMMA TF32 kernel that does not beat cuBLAS TF32.
caveats: The win is cuBLAS's roughly 16 us per-call launch and heuristic floor on tiny matrices, not arithmetic throughput; the license was changed from MIT to a view-only 'all rights reserved' text, so the code cannot be copied; one GPU and one build; compiled with --use_fast_math; the README does not give run counts or variance.
found_via: GitHub repository search 'outperforms cuBLAS'; opened the repo page, README, gemm/README.md, CMakeLists.txt and LICENSE.

name: blackwell-tensorcore-kernels
baseline: cuBLAS FP16-in/FP32-accumulate tensor-core GEMM (cublasGemmEx, which dispatches cutlass_80_tensorop_s16816gemm_f16_128x64 on sm_120)
workload: Hand-written FP16-in/FP32-acc GEMM using raw mma.sync with 3-stage cp.async, XOR swizzle and 64x64 per-warp register tiles, M=N=K=8192 on a Blackwell workstation GPU.
claimed_speedup: 243.2 TFLOP/s vs 229.0 TFLOP/s for cuBLAS tensor-core GEMM at 8192^3 on sm_120 (106.1%); the WMMA kernel in the same repo reaches only 44.4% of it, and a CUTLASS 3.x wgmma build reaches 85.5% of cuBLAS on H100 (641 TFLOP/s).
compiler_and_flags: nvcc from CUDA 12.8 via CMake (C++17; CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES 90 120; sm_120a for FP4 rows); no extra nvcc flags set in CMakeLists.txt
hardware: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q (sm_120, CUDA 12.8); cross-generation rows on an H100 80GB SXM5 (sm_90, CUDA 13.1)
tradeoffs: FP16-in/FP32-acc GEMM only; a teaching/measurement repo with an ablation ladder, not a drop-in library; sm_120 tuned; the Hopper path needs CUTLASS 3.x and sm_90a.
caveats: The 6% win is over the older cutlass_80 kernel that cuBLAS picks on this card (a dispatch gap), at one size, on a power-capped Max-Q part; the README says it is not a cuBLAS replacement and states every other row is below cuBLAS (45% for WMMA, 85.5% for the H100 CUTLASS path); commits are co-authored by an AI assistant per the commit list; baseline cuBLAS is not one of OpenBLAS, MKL, Eigen or BLIS.
found_via: GitHub repository search 'topic:tensor-cores gemm language:Cuda'; opened the repo page, README, CMakeLists.txt, Makefile and commits page.

name: Tiled-MM
baseline: NVIDIA cublasXt (vanilla and manually tuned with 4000 tile size and pinned memory)
workload: Double-precision square column-major GEMM (alpha=beta=1) on matrices stored in host memory, tiled and pipelined to one GPU (also ported to AMD via rocBLAS).
claimed_speedup: README: 'Tiled-MM was substantially faster than the vanilla version of cublasXt, and achieved similar performance as the manually tuned version of cublasXt' (chart image, no numbers in text).
hardware: One node of Piz Daint (Cray XC50) with an NVIDIA P100 GPU
tradeoffs: Host-pointer tiled GEMM for CUDA or ROCm; user-selectable tile size per dimension and stream count; reusable context for repeated calls; templated over data types.
caveats: Plot only, no numbers in the text; the win is over vanilla cublasXt only and it merely matches a hand-tuned cublasXt; compiler and flags not stated; P100-era (2019) data; baseline cublasXt is not one of OpenBLAS, MKL, Eigen or BLIS.
found_via: GitHub topics/matrix-multiplication?l=c++ page (WebFetch); opened the repo page, README and commits page.
